items.title: [cbc.ca] B.C. floods force evacuations, shelter orders as roads close
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Heavy rain and flooding across British Columbia’s South Coast prompted shelter-in-place advisories near Squamish and in Pemberton Valley, while evacuation orders covered parts of Pemberton and Lil’wat Nation on Thursday, Nov. 12. Some areas received more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours, and floodwater closed Highway 99 east of Pemberton and roads near Squamish. The entire Village of Pemberton was under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders also remained in effect in Zeballos, where flooding and landslide risks threatened about 30 properties. The release of water from the Cheakamus Dam flooded roads near Squamish and was intended to make room in the reservoir for more rain. Officials expected river levels to crest Thursday and then recede. Rain eased in some areas, but Vancouver Island remained under rainfall and flood warnings, and forecasters were tracking more storm systems expected over the weekend.

items.title: [phys.org] UN warns warming will breach 1.5C as COP31 opens Monday
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The United Nations says global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold as nearly 200 countries prepare to begin the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9. Climate scientists say the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to become the second year to exceed 1.5C, after 2024. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the world must now limit how far temperatures rise beyond that level and blamed political leaders for failing to act. The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

items.title: [tsln.com] Cattle specialists urge targeted winter feeding to manage costs
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Cattle advisers and researchers are urging producers to match winter rations to forage quality and herd needs. Drought has tightened forage supplies, and feed is a major operating expense. South Dakota State University research found that limit-fed, energy-dense diets reduced feed use and methane emissions without harming calf growth through weaning, saving about $29 per cow. Kansas State University cow-calf specialist Jason Warner recommends assessing forage and supplementing protein as dormant grasses lose quality. French livestock trainer Guillaume Beaure describes reducing feed waste by closely matching rations to animals’ needs. Advisers also recommend checking forage mineral levels because winter hay can pose a risk of magnesium deficiency.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A groundbreaking drone survey has revealed a startling split in the fate of New Zealand's endangered Erect-crested penguins. While one population has remained stable for decades, another has declined by more than 40%, apparently due to a combination of predators, worsening storms, and changing ocean conditions. Even more surprisingly, the tiny Bounty Islands support nearly as many breeding pairs as the Antipodes Islands, despite being 40 times smaller.

items.title: [energynow.com] Norway’s Supreme Court invalidates three oilfield permits over emissions reviews
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Norway’s Supreme Court on Nov. 13 invalidated government approvals for the North Sea oilfields Breidablikk, Tyrving and Yggdrasil, ruling that environmental reviews should have assessed emissions from burning the extracted oil, not just from production. The six-to-five decision requires the Energy Ministry to reconsider the permits under proper procedures but does not order operators to stop work. Equinor’s Breidablikk and Aker BP’s Tyrving are producing, and Yggdrasil is scheduled to start production in 2027. Environmental groups Greenpeace Norway and Young Friends of the Earth brought the case against the state in 2023. The court said the oil companies were not parties to the case, so the ruling does not automatically suspend their operations. The campaigners’ lawyer said they would consider bringing a separate case against the operators. The ministry said it would re-examine the permits. The government has said it has changed its practice to include emissions from burning oil and gas in assessments for new fields.

items.title: [independent.co.uk] Super El Niño warms Pacific, threatens California marine life and snowpack
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Climate Prediction Center said the developing El Niño is likely to remain strong to very strong through March 2027, with ocean temperatures still rising. The event is already associated with unusually warm waters off California, higher coastal water levels and changes in marine food supplies. Scientists report seabirds washing ashore and kelp forests under stress. The pattern can shift rainfall and temperature, and forecasters expect warmer winters in the Northwest that could reduce snowpack by raising snow levels. Scientists also warn that warm Pacific waters can increase the risk of coastal flooding when high tides coincide with storms. NOAA’s outlook says the event is expected to weaken early next year, while reports indicate its effects could continue into spring.

A preliminary assessment of the post-wildfire hazards of the Pear Lake wildfire near Clinton this past summer show that homes, highways, and infrastructure such as the CN rail line and a BC Hydro substation are at elevated risk from flooding, debris flows, and landslides in the fire’s aftermath. The Pear Lake wildfire was reported on July 17, and was not declared under control until Sept. 14. It burned a total area of 165,909 hectares (1,659 square kilometres), forced the evacuation of thousands of residents, and destroyed more than 120 structures, including homes. The report — dated Oct. 8 and released on Nov. 9 — is largely based on aerial reconnaissance carried out in August. The report’s author, geomorphologist Sarah Crookshanks, notes that it was prepared on an expedited basis so that a Level 4 Detailed Assessment can be started. The fire affected 28 watersheds, with some seeing up to 99 per cent of their area burned. items.title: [zmescience.com] Researchers will track marine life on sunken SS United States liner
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Researchers at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution plan a multiyear study of the SS United States, the retired ocean liner deliberately sunk off Florida to form an artificial reef. The project will document how a marine community develops on the ship, with initial surveys planned within the first month after its Nov. 11 sinking. The team plans to collect water samples at 132 locations around the wreck and monitor microbial communities and marine life while tracking metals — including iron, manganese and nickel — released as the steel corrodes. Researchers say the development of a reef ecosystem is seldom observed from its earliest stages. The SS United States Preservation Foundation challenged the reef’s environmental safety before the sinking. It argued that deteriorating hull coatings could release chromium and zinc and that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers had not fully assessed the environmental effects. A federal judge rejected its request to block the sinking on Nov. 6 but allowed it to refile.

items.content_html:

Amy Pope, director general of the International Organization for Migration (IOM), warned at the United Nations climate conference, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, that more than 200 million people living in highly climate-vulnerable communities are at risk of displacement. IOM data show storms, drought, wildfires, extreme temperatures and floods forced nearly 30 million people from their homes in 2025. Pope said governments spend billions of dollars on border security while underfunding adaptation measures that could help communities remain in place. She estimated the cost of those measures at about $310 billion, compared with roughly $30 billion in funding so far. She argued that helping communities adapt before displacement occurs is more humane and cost-effective than responding to irregular migration after it begins.

items.title: [spacewatch.global] ESA's Euclid opens 1.7-petabyte archive as processing demands grow
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The European Space Agency and the Euclid Consortium opened a 1.7-petabyte archive on Nov. 12, releasing 13 months of observations from the space telescope’s first major survey stage. The archive catalogs more than 900 million galaxies, includes about 15,000 strong gravitational-lens candidates and provides spectra for more than 160 million sources. The observations cover 1,900 square degrees, about 14% of the area planned for Euclid’s six-year survey. Processing the data places heavy demands on computing centers, and the Max Planck Society said limited availability of new hardware adds to the workload. The complete Data Release 1, scheduled for June 16, 2027, is expected to add higher-level products for studying galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing. Euclid’s full map is planned to cover more than one-third of the sky by 2031.

Cyber incidents targeting operational technology (OT) systems—the controllers that monitor and operate physical equipment—have disrupted refrigeration, water and energy operations, often through exposed or outdated devices. Attacks on European supermarket refrigeration systems caused food spoilage, while incidents affecting U.S. water utilities and Polish energy organizations disrupted monitoring and control. Isolating a compromised system can cut operators off from equipment-status information they need to make safe decisions, according to a Communications of the ACM contributor. Finland’s Transport and Communications Agency said household smart devices were not targets in the European refrigeration attacks, but advised users to secure routers and connected devices.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] German parliament gives spy agencies powers to hack, sabotage and enter homes
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Germany’s Bundestag voted on Nov. 13 to give the foreign intelligence service BND and domestic intelligence agency BfV new powers to disrupt threats, including cyber operations and, under certain conditions, covert entry into homes and business premises. The measure passed 309-190, with 71 abstentions. The government says it responds to foreign espionage and sabotage, including activity it attributes to Russia. The BND will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, while the BfV may take action against property and computer systems when it identifies specific threats. The agencies also gain expanded digital surveillance tools, including access to encrypted communications and AI-assisted data analysis. Arrests and overt searches remain police responsibilities, and an independent oversight body will review certain intrusive measures in advance. The government says the reform equips Germany to counter hybrid attacks; critics warn it weakens the postwar boundary between intelligence gathering and police powers. Modernizing the agencies under the bill will take years, and the Financial Times reported that recruitment in key areas is already proving difficult.

items.title: [scimex.org] Astronomers trace eight-minute radio pulses to white dwarf and Sun-like star
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Astronomers have traced repeating radio pulses from the system GPM J071507−114153 to a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like star—the first known long-period radio transient with this type of stellar pairing. The pulses recur every 7.9 minutes but appear only during a roughly six-hour window in each 32-hour orbit. The system lies more than 5,000 light-years away. Researchers discovered the system using Australia’s Murchison Widefield Array, pinpointed it with South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope and used the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii to identify the companion as a G-type star. Measurements of the orbit and the companion’s slight movement indicate that the pulsing object has about two-thirds the Sun’s mass, making it too light to be a neutron star. The study was published in Nature Astronomy on Nov. 12, 2026.

items.title: [popsci.com] Nearby giant likely tilted hot Jupiter out of view
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

items.title: [ogj.com] IEA says diesel supply remains tight as Gulf exports recover
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The International Energy Agency (IEA) says Gulf oil shipments have recovered enough to lift crude supply, but damaged supply routes and limited refinery output continue to constrain diesel and other refined fuels. Gulf exports excluding Oman reached 18.4 million barrels a day in October, still 26% below prewar levels, as attacks on tankers continued. Producers shipped oil through the Strait of Hormuz, with tankers switching off tracking signals to avoid detection. European diesel was near $180 a barrel in October, about 77% above prewar levels, while refinery processing fell by 1.3 million barrels a day from September to 81.3 million as seasonal maintenance peaked. The IEA also said continued attacks on Russian energy infrastructure have restricted diesel exports, adding to losses from the Middle East. To ease the shortfall, IEA member countries plan to release another 71 million barrels of emergency oil and products by the end of February 2027, including about 15 million barrels of diesel, mostly from French and German government stocks. The agency said the diesel releases are intended to cover the shortfall until refinery operations and product output recover.

items.title: [Fast Company] A cyberattack forces you to pull the plug. Can your business keep running?
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The recent cyberattack on European supermarkets sent the temperature in some Swedish freezers to a sweltering 131 F (55 C). The Dutch grocery chain Ahold Delhaize warned that a separate hack could strip up to 250 million euros ($277 million) from sales, and wipe as much as 100 million euros off operating profit in the fourth quarter. 

This recent spate of cyberattacks around the world, including a staggering $6.3 billion heist at the crypto exchange Binance, lays bare a blind spot in many boardrooms. Directors too often ask whether attackers can break into their systems. They should also be asking whether the business can take the hit and keep running.

Boards should assume attackers will get through. It’s a question of when, not if. And when they do, can the business still fulfill orders, pay staff, and keep critical facilities open? 

Too rare

Unfortunately, this is often not the case in the companies that I deal with. I recently worked with a board that had rightly grown more worried about cyber threats, and drafted in a former spy to carry out a cyber audit. The contractor ran penetration tests, hacked a few of the firm’s products, and found holes in its defenses. 

That’s fairly typical. The audit tested whether hackers could penetrate the company’s defenses. But it stopped short of testing whether the business could ride out a breach. And this is the gap I see running through many companies. 

Sometimes, stopping an attack from spreading means shutting down the very systems that keep you operating. 

Ahold Delhaize took some of its own websites and apps down as a precaution after the cyberattack, cutting off online shopping for some customers. The Dutch group contained most of the disruption within two weeks and it was getting back to normal once it reported third-quarter results. In Belgium, it had online shopping back up and running just a week after disclosing the breach. 

Contrast that with Marks & Spencer, the British retail stalwart. After a breach in April 2025, it stopped taking online clothing orders for a spell of 46 days. And when orders finally resumed, only part of its clothing range was available.

If you have to pull the plug on your own systems to contain a breach, how will you keep serving customers? 

The AI factor

AI is only raising the stakes. It’s my view that cyber threats have changed more in the past six months than in the previous six years. But many companies haven’t caught up.

Some of the newest crop of AI models are spotting security flaws that their predecessors missed, and have worked out how to exploit some of them. 

Take Anthropic’s Mythos Preview, which scored about 83% on a cybersecurity benchmark, compared with roughly 67% for the company’s previous best model, Claude Opus 4.6. Anthropic says it spotted thousands of security flaws, many of them serious, including in every major operating system and web browser. Worrying indeed. 

Last week, OpenAI released GPT‑6 Cyber to vetted customers. The model is designed to find security flaws and test whether they can be exploited.

The U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre says the gap between a flaw becoming public and attackers exploiting it has already shrunk to just days. And it predicts that AI will compress that window further still, giving defenders even less time to patch the holes.

The most recent spate of supermarket hacks came on the heels of a similar hack of fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets. The result was piles of spoiled food, and fires even broke out.

Following that breach, Danfoss, the Danish industrial company that made the temperature controls, urged its customers to update their software and hardware. But just weeks later, hackers hit retailers using Danfoss controls again. This time, stores in several European countries were hit, including Sweden and Ireland.

Some fared better than others. Carrefour said it had installed updates and secured its connections after the first wave of attacks, steps it credited with curbing the numbers of its Belgian stores hit. Acting on the first warning helped Carrefour blunt the next attack.

Some retailers left their refrigeration systems exposed. That’s unacceptable. But even with tighter security, you still need a way to trade when the systems you depend on go dark.

What to do

Protect the operations you can least afford to lose. Then drill your teams on how to keep them running through an attack. When the malware designated NotPetya hit Maersk in 2017, the shipping giant handled about 80% of its usual volume manually. Staff taped paperwork to containers and took orders through personal Gmail accounts.

Consider a distribution center that needs to keep essential goods moving. Ask one team to fulfill a handful of priority orders without its usual order system or company email. Can staff confirm orders using a secure offline list and an agreed backup channel, check stock by hand and arrange transport? Have them log each dispatch on paper and check those logs against the order system once it’s back online.

When the drill ends, ask how much of the usual workload the team handled safely, for how long, and where it got stuck. Give each fix an owner and a deadline, then run the drill again.

Find out how long you can keep serving customers with your systems down. A real attack is a brutal way to get the answer.

MIT researchers found that older adults had significantly weaker waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which helps clear waste from the brain during sleep, than younger adults. Separately, a study described in a paper shared on Reddit found that LSD-related gene-expression patterns in rats and mice ran counter to some patterns associated with human brain aging. LSD also reduced certain amyloid-beta-related changes in mouse brain-cell cultures. These are preclinical findings, not evidence that LSD prevents dementia in people.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Canadian police suspend use of Crime Stoppers after 1.5 million records exposed
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Canadian police services are suspending their use of Crime Stoppers after a breach exposed more than 1.5 million tips submitted across Canada over 25 years, a CBC News investigation found. More than 850,000 records included personally identifiable information. The tips were managed through P3, software provided by U.S.-based Navigate360. Navigate360 acknowledged on Friday that its database had been breached between November 2025 and March 2026 and said potentially exposed information included names, addresses, birth dates and Social Security numbers. The company said it had no evidence the information had been used for fraud or identity theft. Police in several provinces have paused their use of the service while they assess the breach and its safeguards. Toronto and Ottawa police are directing people to report information through police channels, which do not necessarily offer the same anonymity. Crime Stoppers chapters and police are seeking further details from Navigate360. The company said it hired a cybersecurity firm to help strengthen security.

items.title: [sciencefeatured.com] Higher BMI over time linked to faster cognitive decline in older adults
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A 24-year study of several thousand middle-aged and older Americans found that higher average body mass index (BMI) over time was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking. A team led by University of Georgia researcher Suhang Song reported the findings in the Journal of Neurology. The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began. The observational study cannot establish that higher weight causes cognitive decline or that weight loss would prevent it. The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity. The team called for further research into possible biological mechanisms and future interventions.

items.title: [phoronix.com] Linux developer releases XRAID parity RAID integrated with XFS
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Linux developer Christoph Hellwig has released XRAID, a declustered parity RAID implementation integrated with the XFS file system and designed especially for zoned storage devices such as shingled magnetic recording drives. XRAID also works with conventional hard drives and SSDs. Early figures cited by Hellwig indicate writes can be up to 20 times faster than Linux’s mdraid, though SSD performance was not a focus. The code has been in development for 18 months and is available for wider testing, but Hellwig said it is not ready for submission to the Linux kernel. Its kernel patches are under review on the mailing list, while an xfsprogs branch supports file-system creation and provides a new management utility.

Data layout: XRAID applies parity to file data stored in XFS realtime groups, while stacked Linux drivers such as MD RAID mirroring can handle metadata redundancy separately (phoronix.com).
